blocks.content: Aeolian soils are formed by wind transportation, where saltation is the predominant mechanism for moving medium-sized sand grains.

rows: Fine dust and silt floating in atmospheric air currents over long distances.
Sand grains moving in a series of short bouncing or jumping trajectories near the ground.
Coarser particles rolling or sliding along the surface due to impacts from saltating grains.

items: Loess is frequently tested in GATE and ESE as a classic example of an aeolian silt deposit with high collapsibility upon saturation.
Questions often test particle size thresholds: Suspension (<0.1 mm), Saltation (0.1 mm to 0.5 mm), and Surface Creep (>0.5 mm).
Aeolian deposits are characterized as uniformly graded (poorly graded) soils due to the natural sorting action of wind.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Wind transportation (Aeolian process) moves soil particles through three distinct mechanisms: suspension, saltation, and surface creep.
Saltation is the dominant mode of wind transport, responsible for moving 50% to 75% of wind-borne sediment weight through bouncing motions.
Loess is a major aeolian deposit composed of wind-blown silt particles, characterized by light color, high compressibility, and collapsible behavior upon wetting.
Sand dunes are deposits of fine to medium sand formed when wind encounters obstacles, leading to uniform-graded soil accumulation.
Aeolian soils typically exhibit poor grading (uniform particle size distribution) because wind sorts particles selectively by size and weight.
